abstract.para: RAID implies several strategies for combining several hard disks in a RAID system, each with different goals, advantages, and characteristics. These variations are commonly known as RAID levels.

topic.para: The RAID levels can be split into the following categories:

listitem.para: These levels and their associated data formats are standardized by the Storage Networking Industry Association (SNIA) in the Common RAID Disk Drive Format (DDF) standard. The standard RAID levels are RAID 0, RAID 1, RAID 2, RAID 3, RAID 4, RAID 5 and RAID 6. For details, refer to .
Usually, these are proprietary RAID configurations designed to meet specific needs, for example, Linux MD RAID 10.

section.title: Standard RAID levels
section.para: Originally, there were only five standard levels of RAID, but other levels have evolved.

To calculate the usable storage capacity of a software RAID array, let N represent the total number of active disks in the array (excluding hot spares), and C represent the capacity of a single disk, assuming all disks are of equal size. If disk sizes vary, C is limited to the capacity of the smallest disk in the array. For RAID 10 configurations, r represents the redundancy factor (number of data copies), which defaults to 2 in standard mirrored pairs.

table.title: RAID Levels and Usable Storage Capacity Formulas

row.entry: 100% usable capacity; no parity or mirroring overhead.
Usable capacity equals a single disk, regardless of how many mirrors (N) are added.
With standard 2-way mirroring (r = 2), usable capacity is 50% of total raw storage.
Equivalent of one disk is dedicated to a single parity drive.
Equivalent of one disk is allocated to distributed single parity.
Equivalent of two disks is allocated to distributed dual parity.

section.title: RAID 0
section.para: RAID 0 improves the performance of your data operations by spreading out blocks of each file across multiple disks. This data distributions is called striping. The overall capacity is a sum of capacity of disk in the RAID. The benefit of RAID 0 is that the throughput of read and write operations to any file is multiplied by the number of drives because reads and writes are done concurrently.
The disadvantage of RAID 0 is that it does not provide any data backup, so if a disk fails, the whole RAID is destroyed and there is data loss.

section.title: RAID 1
section.para: RAID 1 provides adequate security for your data, because the data is copied to another hard disk 1:1. This is known as hard disk mirroring. RAID 1 does not use data striping, so write performance is not improved compared to a single drive. However, read throughput can increase because the system can read independent data blocks concurrently from multiple mirrored disks. Additionally, the array continues to operate as long as at least one drive is functioning.
RAID 1 requires at least two devices.

section.title: RAID 4
section.para: RAID 4 provides block-level striping with a dedicated parity drive. If a data disk fails, the parity data is used to create a replacement disk. However, the parity disk might create a bottleneck for write access. This level requires at least three devices.
RAID 4 is not commonly used in practice.

section.title: RAID 5
section.para: RAID 5 provides a balance between performance, capacity, and redundancy by using block-level striping with single distributed parity. Data and parity information are distributed evenly across all drives. Parity is calculated using XOR math across the data blocks, allowing the system to reconstruct data if a single drive fails.

Usable storage capacity equals the total number of drives minus one (N-1), assuming all drives are of equal size. RAID 5 can sustain a maximum of one drive failure without data loss; a failed drive should be replaced promptly to restore fault tolerance. RAID 5 requires a minimum of three disks (two data disks and one parity disk).

section.title: RAID 6
section.para: RAID 6 uses the same striping and parity mechanism as RAID 5, but calculates double distributed parity across the drives. This dual-parity scheme enables the array to sustain up to two simultaneous drive failures without data loss.

Usable storage capacity equals the total number of drives minus two (N-2), assuming all drives are of equal size. Performance is comparable to RAID 5 under normal operations, though write operations require additional CPU overhead to calculate the second parity block. RAID 6 requires a minimum of four disks (two data disks and two parity disks).

section.title: RAID 10
section.para: RAID 10 (also known as RAID 1+0 or a stripe of mirrors) is a hybrid RAID configuration that combines the high-speed performance of RAID 0 striping with the fault-tolerant redundancy of RAID 1 mirroring. Requiring a minimum of four drives (and always an even total number of drives, $N$), it first pairs drives into mirrored sets to protect data and then stripes data across those pairs to accelerate read and write operations.

While this architecture sacrifices half of the raw storage capacity—yielding a usable capacity of $(N / 2) \times C—it delivers exceptional I/O performance, rapid rebuild times, and high resilience, surviving multiple drive failures as long as no single mirrored pair loses both of its drives.
